rationale: Darius orders the archive search that the governors requested when asking whether Cyrus had authorized the Jerusalem temple.
The discovered memorandum answers the earlier request for a search; the requested Babylon treasury search and the actual discovery in a Median citadel remain distinct locations.
The recovered memorandum attributes the temple-building authorization to Cyrus's first year, matching the earlier proclamation's king, date and Jerusalem temple commission.

The memorandum specifies stone and timber courses, while the governors' report describes selected stones and timber already being used in the temple walls; this compares the authorized materials with the reported work without equating every architectural detail.
The memorandum orders the return of the vessels Nebuchadnezzar removed from Jerusalem, and the earlier account describes Cyrus releasing those vessels through Mithradates to Sasabasar.
The order addresses the governor and Satharbouzana's associates who had questioned the builders and sent the report to Darius.
The governor's inquiry concerned the elders' authority to rebuild; Darius now commands that the elders be allowed to rebuild on the temple's site.
Darius's order funds the temple through royal revenues beyond the river; the later Arthasastha decree likewise directs royal treasuries to provide for the temple. These are distinct royal grants.

The decree supplies cattle, rams, lambs, grain, wine and oil for temple worship; Numbers prescribes animal offerings with flour, oil and wine. The comparison explains the sacrificial supplies without treating every requested item as a quotation.

The decree asks for prayer for the king and his sons; the later instruction explicitly calls for prayers for kings and those in authority, providing a specific thematic parallel in intercession for rulers.
Darius invokes the God whose name dwells at the Jerusalem house; Deuteronomy connects the chosen place bearing God's name with the presentation of sacrifices and offerings there.
Thanthanai and Satharbouzana, named as the senders of the earlier letter, now carry out the king's response.
The completion summary names Haggai and Zacharias son of Addo, the prophets already shown helping the restored temple's builders.
Haggai describes the people hearing his message and resuming work on the Lord's house under Darius, supplying concrete context for Ezra's statement that the elders built through Haggai's prophecy.

Zechariah is identified through Addo and dated under Darius, and his vision promises the rebuilding of God's house in Jerusalem; this supports the prophetic context named in Ezra without claiming that the entire vision is quoted.
Haggai dates work on the temple to Darius's second year, while Ezra dates its completion to his sixth year; the passages mark distinct stages of the rebuilding.

The returned community joyfully dedicates God's house with offerings, recalling the earlier dedication of Solomon's temple with Israel's sacrifices and rejoicing; the two dedications remain distinct events.

Ezra's dedication includes twelve male goats for sin on behalf of Israel's tribes; the altar-dedication totals in Numbers likewise include twelve male goats for sin. The other quantities and the occasions differ.
Ezra expressly appeals to the book of Moses for temple service; Numbers assigns the Levites to assist Aaron and his sons and places the priests over their appointed sanctuary duties.
The returned community keeps Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, the precise date prescribed in Leviticus.
Both narratives describe purified priests and Levites and Levites slaughtering Passover for the assembled people; the earlier celebration occurred in the second month and is not the same event.

Ezra includes people separating themselves from the surrounding nations' uncleanness to seek Israel's God; Exodus permits resident foreigners to join Passover under its stated covenant requirements. Ezra does not repeat all of those requirements.
The community's seven-day Festival of Unleavened Bread follows the duration prescribed in Leviticus.
Ezra attributes royal support for the temple to the Lord turning the king's heart; Proverbs explicitly depicts a king's heart as directed by God.

Ezra's ancestry names Saraias, Azarias and Elkia in descending ancestral order; Chronicles places Saraias after Azariah and Chelkias in the priestly line. The comparison does not turn the condensed ancestry into a complete list of immediate generations.

Ezra's ancestral sequence Saloum, Saddouk and Achitob corresponds in reverse genealogical direction to Chronicles' Achitob, Sadok and Salom within the priestly line; each passage's spellings are preserved.

Ezra traces his ancestry through Abisoue, Phinees and Eleazar to Aaron; Chronicles supplies the corresponding Aaron-Eleazar-Phinees-Abisou line, without identifying Ezra with any person merely sharing a name.

relationship: Ezra's role as teacher of the law
rationale: Ezra is introduced as a priestly scribe skilled in Moses' law; Nehemiah later presents Esdras the priest and scribe bringing that law and reading it before the people.

The later return includes priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and Nathinim, the same distinct service groups named in the earlier settlement summary; this does not equate the members of the two returning groups.
The dated arrival notice is expanded by the account of departure from Aoue and arrival in Jerusalem; no identity between the first-month planning date and the later departure day is imposed.
The journey summary attributes the successful ascent to God's good hand, and the later travel account describes that hand protecting the travelers before they reach Jerusalem.
Ezra's resolve to study, do and teach the law is concretely illustrated by the later public reading and explanation through which the assembly understands God's law.
The introduction identifies a decree given to Ezra the priest and scribe; its concluding commands appoint him to establish judges and teach and enforce the law.
The address names Ezra as scribe of the law of the God of heaven, and the decree later repeats that distinctive office while directing treasurers to supply his requests.

Arthasastha permits willing Israelites and temple personnel to go to Jerusalem with Ezra; Cyrus's earlier decree similarly authorizes return and support for the Jerusalem house. The decrees belong to different returns and rulers.
The decree entrusts the king's and advisers' silver and gold offering to Ezra; the later weighing explicitly includes gifts from the king and his advisers.

The authorized voluntary contributions from Babylon's people and priests correspond to the later consignment that includes offerings from the Israelites present there, without treating every donor category as an identical enumeration.
The decree funds bulls, rams, lambs and their accompanying sacrifices and drink offerings; Numbers specifies those animal offerings together with flour, oil and wine.

The decree directs the remaining silver and gold to uses pleasing to God; Ezra later identifies the transported silver and gold as holy freewill offerings and entrusts them to priests and Levites for delivery to the temple.
The order to hand over the vessels at Jerusalem is followed by their transport and their counted and weighed delivery at God's house.

Arthasastha authorizes supplies from royal treasuries for the temple's needs, following the earlier policy under Darius of funding construction and requested sacrificial provisions; the grants remain distinct.
The order to treasuries beyond the river belongs to the royal ordinance that the travelers later deliver to the king's administrators and governors in that region.
The quantified authorization of wheat, wine, oil and salt parallels Darius's earlier provision of those same supplies at the priests' request; the quantities are not equated across decrees.

Arthasastha's concern to avert wrath from the king and his sons parallels Darius's request for offerings and prayer for the life of the king and his sons, linking royal support with the welfare of the royal household.
Ezra is commissioned to appoint officials and judges under God's law; Deuteronomy specifically commands appointed judges and recording officers to administer righteous judgment.

The decree sanctions refusal to obey God's law and the king's law; Deuteronomy requires obedience to priestly and judicial rulings and penalizes presumptuous refusal. The decree's several penalties are not all attributed to this passage of Torah.
Ezra blesses God for putting the glorification of the Jerusalem temple into the king's heart, corresponding to the proverb that God directs a king's heart.
Ezra says he gathered Israelite leaders to accompany him, and the next chapter introduces the list of family leaders who went up with him under Arthasastha.
The list of leaders who went up with Ezra supplies the concrete continuation of his statement that he gathered Israelite leaders for the journey.

The return list includes a man from the sons of Ithamar; Chronicles identifies Ithamar as an Aaronic priestly branch with its own ancestral houses. This supplies family background without identifying the returning Daniel with another bearer of that name.
Both return lists explicitly contain the sons of Phoros. This connects the named family across the two returns, without equating the travelers or their differing totals.
Both lists explicitly identify a group as sons of Phaathmoab; the later leader and his two hundred companions are not equated with the earlier return's larger group.
The sons of Adin appear in both returns. The shared family designation supports the connection while the named later leader and differing group counts remain distinct.
The sons of Saphatia are recorded in both returns; the link is between the expressly named family groups, not an assertion that the individual travelers are the same.
Both lists explicitly name the sons of Babi. The later group under Zacharia is connected at the family level without conflating its seventy-eight members with the earlier total.
The sons of Asgad appear in both return lists, providing the family connection; the later leader and one hundred and ten companions remain distinct from the earlier group.
Both returns name the sons of Adonikam, and the later entry adds its own leaders and sixty companions. The connection does not force the two group totals to agree.
Ezra initially finds no Levites among those gathered for departure; the subsequent arrival notice identifies the Levitical family groups recruited to remedy that absence.

The named messengers are sent with instructions to obtain personnel for God's house, and the next verses describe the resulting arrivals; their names are not equated with similarly named men elsewhere.

The instructions call for service personnel through the Nathinim, and the ensuing report records the arrival of two hundred and twenty Nathinim. The unusual wording about the place is preserved without emendation.
The arrival under God's good hand follows Ezra's discovery that Levites were absent and his resulting recruitment mission; the link does not attempt to resolve every compressed ancestral name.

The arriving men are expressly from the sons of Merari; Chronicles places Merari among Levi's sons and names that branch's ancestral families, without identifying the individual arrivals with earlier namesakes.

The recorded Nathinim arrivals answer the preceding mission to obtain personnel for God's house through their brothers the Nathinim; the link does not supply an unrecorded account of David's original appointment.
The fast seeks a safe way for the travelers, children and property; the departure account later credits God's hand with rescue from enemies along the way.

Ezra declines to request troops and horsemen because of his testimony about God's protection, whereas Nehemiah receives commanders and horsemen and likewise credits God's good hand. The texts describe distinct journeys and different practical provisions.
Ezra explains that God's good hand rests on those seeking Him and His wrath on those abandoning Him; Azarias likewise contrasts seeking God and finding Him with forsaking Him and being forsaken.
The statement that God heard their fasting and petition refers back to the declared fast for a safe journey for the community and its possessions.
Ezra sets apart priestly leaders before entrusting them with the offerings; the later instructions require guarded transport and record priests and Levites accepting custody.
The weighed consignment explicitly comes from the king, advisers, leaders and Israelites, continuing the decree's provision for royal and voluntary communal gifts to the temple.

The silver and gold weighed into the custodians' hands are later delivered at the temple by number and weight; the link concerns custody and accounting, not an invented correspondence between every total.
The listed gold and bronze vessels belong to the entrusted consignment later weighed and counted at God's house; the source's unfamiliar vessel and measure terms remain unchanged.

Ezra calls the bearers and vessels holy, while Isaiah calls those carrying the Lord's vessels to separate from uncleanness and promises God's protection in departure. This is a specific thematic connection, not a claim that Ezra quotes the prophecy verbatim.
The command to guard the valuables until delivery before Jerusalem's leaders is followed by their weighed and recorded handover at the temple.
The priests and Levites receive the vessels for transport to Jerusalem, carrying forward the royal instruction to hand the vessels over there before God.
God's rescue from enemies during the journey is the concrete protection for which the travelers had fasted and prayed before setting out.
The arrival and three-day stay expand the earlier summary that Ezra's company reached Jerusalem in the fifth month under God's good hand.
The temple handover to named recipients completes the transport of the silver, gold and vessels earlier weighed out and placed under priestly and Levitical custody.
The final record of every item by number and weight corresponds to the earlier itemized weighing of the silver, gold and vessels before departure.

relationship: offerings on behalf of all Israel
rationale: The new arrivals offer twelve young bulls for all Israel and twelve male goats for sin; the earlier dedication likewise used twelve male goats for sin according to Israel's tribes. The other offerings and their quantities differ.
The travelers deliver the king's ordinance to regional officials, continuing the decree's directions to treasuries beyond the river concerning temple provision and the service personnel.

The leaders charge Israel with sharing the surrounding peoples' repulsive practices; Deuteronomy names several of those peoples and commands separation from their covenants, intermarriage and worship. The two lists of peoples are not treated as identical.
The complaint that Israelites and their sons have married surrounding peoples' daughters directly engages Deuteronomy's prohibition and its warning that such marriages turn sons away from God.
Ezra's torn garments and grief over the reported breach are continued by his later refusal of food and water while mourning that same communal unfaithfulness.
The initial gathering around Ezra during his distress develops into the large assembly that gathers while he prays, confesses and weeps over the breach.
Ezra kneels and stretches his hands toward God in prayer concerning Israel's sins; Solomon is likewise described kneeling with hands spread toward heaven after interceding for Israel at the temple.
Ezra confesses overwhelming collective guilt and shame before God; Daniel's prayer likewise assigns shame of face to Israel, its rulers and fathers because of their sins.

Ezra recalls ancestral unfaithfulness leading to sword, captivity and plunder; Chronicles narrates the leaders', priests' and people's breaches, followed by killing, temple plunder and Babylonian deportation.

Ezra acknowledges God's renewed favor in preserving survivors and restoring a sanctuary foothold; Jeremiah promises God's visitation and return from Babylon. The target uses the pinned translation's chapter numbering.
Ezra's prayer credits God with mercy through Persian rulers for restoration of the temple; Cyrus's proclamation supplies an earlier concrete instance of that royal authorization and support.
The prayer's reference to restoring God's desolate house looks back to the completion account that names the Persian royal decrees under which it was rebuilt.
Ezra asks what can be said after abandoning God's commands; Daniel likewise confesses refusal to hear God's voice and abandonment of the law, in the setting of communal penitential prayer.

Ezra's confession describes the inherited land filled with the peoples' uncleanness and abominations; Leviticus explicitly connects those practices with the land's defilement and warns Israel against repeating them.

The prohibition against giving daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for sons closely repeats Deuteronomy's intermarriage prohibition; the rest of Ezra's combined exhortation is not assigned to that one passage.

Ezra's instruction never to seek their peace or good corresponds to Deuteronomy's prohibition on seeking the peace or advantage of Ammonites and Moabites; Deuteronomy's stated scope is preserved rather than silently extended to every nation.

Ezra acknowledges deserved calamity yet surviving deliverance; Nehemiah's confession likewise recalls being handed to other peoples while God's compassion kept Him from making a complete end of Israel.
Ezra fears destruction after returning to prohibited intermarriage; Deuteronomy directly joins its intermarriage prohibition to the warning of God's kindled wrath and destruction.
Ezra declares God righteous while the surviving people stand guilty; Daniel similarly contrasts God's righteousness with Israel's shame in a confession about communal sin.
The assembly gathers during Ezra's confession, whose content and posture have just been narrated in the preceding chapter.
Sechenias acknowledges settling foreign wives among the community, accepting the specific intermarriage charge that the leaders had first reported to Ezra.

relationship: proposed response to the intermarriage prohibition
rationale: The proposed covenant seeks to address marriages forbidden by the command recalled in Ezra's prayer; Deuteronomy prohibits those marriages but does not itself state this proposal's expulsion of wives and children.
Sechenias urges Ezra to arise and act with the community's support; Ezra then rises and binds the leaders and people by oath to the proposed action.

Ezra makes the community swear to the proposed reform; Nehemiah describes a communal oath to God's law that specifically includes refusal of intermarriage. The two assemblies and their detailed commitments remain distinct.
Ezra's fasting and mourning continue his earlier grief over the deported community's covenant breach; no identity for Ioanan is inferred from a shared name elsewhere.
The proclamation summons the deported community to Jerusalem within three days, and the subsequent account records Judah and Benjamin gathering there within that period.

The assembly summons threatens loss of property and exclusion; the royal commission had authorized Ezra to administer judgment, including loss of property. Exclusion is not claimed to be explicitly listed in that decree.
The community's gathering within three days fulfills the proclamation's stated deadline, while the date and winter conditions belong to this particular assembly.

relationship: public statement of the reported offense
rationale: Ezra publicly names the same intermarriage breach that the leaders had initially reported to him.

Ezra calls for separation from foreign wives, carrying forward Sechenias's acknowledged breach and proposal; the link concerns the narrative's stated response without importing an unstated legal command.
The assembly's affirmative answer continues the community's earlier oath to act on the proposed reform.
The request for more time cites the wintry season and inability to remain outside, explaining the winter conditions already described when the assembly gathered.
The request for leaders to handle cases at appointed times is followed by the selection of family leaders, the opening of examinations and their later completion.
The selection of named family leaders and beginning of examinations implement the assembly's request for an organized process under its leaders.
The completion date closes the examinations established after the assembly requested a scheduled procedure and selected responsible leaders; the source does not give each individual case's outcome.

The offending priests are placed among the sons of Iesous son of Iosedek and his brothers, the expressly named priestly household associated earlier with rebuilding the altar; no individual sons are equated with unrelated namesakes.

The priests' pledge includes a ram concerning their offense; Leviticus prescribes a ram as a guilt offering for a breach of the commandments. This does not make the surrounding pledge to dismiss wives a quotation from that law.
The sons of Emmer appear in the earlier list of returning priests and again in the reform's priestly list. The connection concerns the named priestly family, not identity of every listed member.
The reform's sons of Phasour correspond to the returning priestly family listed as sons of Phassour; the individual later offenders are not identified with unnamed members of the earlier group.

relationship: named family in the restored community
rationale: The reform names men from the sons of Phoros, the same explicit family designation found in the earlier return list; the two lists have different purposes and do not identify the same individuals.

relationship: named family in the restored community
rationale: The reform's men from the sons of Babi belong to the family designation also present in the return list, without equating the named later men with particular earlier travelers.

relationship: named family in the restored community
rationale: The sons of Banoui are explicitly named in both the return inventory and the reform list; this establishes a family connection, not individual equivalences based on shared personal names.

relationship: named family in the restored community
rationale: The sons of Phaathmoab are listed in both the earlier return and the later reform, while the personal names and purposes of the lists remain distinct.
The reform places these sons of Eram among Israel rather than the priests; the earlier list likewise has a non-priestly sons-of-Eram entry, separate from its priestly sons of Erem.

relationship: named family in the restored community
rationale: The sons of Nabou occur in both the earlier return inventory and the later reform list; the link does not identify the later named men with specific unnamed returnees.

relationship: same-chapter scope of the breach and proposal
rationale: The closing notice confirms that the listed men had foreign wives and children, the household situation addressed in the initial proposal; it does not itself narrate the dismissal of each household.
